name: AMC Linear Disability Score
description: "The AMC Linear Disability Score (ALDS) project aims to construct an item bank to measure the functional status of patients with a broad range of stable, chronic diseases"
description_reference: Holman, Rebecca, et al. “Constructing an Item Bank Using Item Response Theory: The AMC Linear Disability Score Project.” Health Services and Outcomes Research Methodology [Dordrecht], vol. 4, no. 1, March 2003, pp. 19–33, https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1025824810390.
plain-language_description: The AMC Linear Disability Score (ALDS) is a non-disease-specific item bank designed to measure a person’s ability to perform activities of daily living, ranging from simple to complex tasks. Questions can be selected from the larger item bank to match the person's level of ability. Responses are scored using  Item Response Theory, which considers the difficulty of each question, rather than simply adding scores together. This allows the ALDS to measure a wide range of functional ability and helps reduce floor and ceiling effects. Higher scores indicate greater ability to carry out everyday activities independently.

name: Barthel Index
description: "The Barthel Index (BI; Mahoney & Barthel, 1965) was developed as a measure of disability in people whose impairment interfered with independent use of their limbs. The BI includes the 10 activities of daily living (self-care and mobility) that are commonly included in activities of daily living (ADL) checklists and physical function instruments. A number of studies (e.g., Loewen & Anderson, 1988) have indicated excellent intra- and interrater reliability for the BI."
description_reference: https://psycnet.apa.org/doi/10.1037/t02366-000
plain-language_description: A tool to rank a patient's independence in 10 areas of daily living, such as feeding, bathing, dressing and mobility.

name: Brain Injury Community Rehabilitation Outcome-39
description: "Construction and validation of a new instrument, the Brain Injury Community Rehabilitation Outcome scales, to assess problems experienced by brain-injured patients living in the community."
description_reference: Powell JH, Beckers K, Greenwood RJ. Measuring progress and outcome in community rehabilitation after brain injury with a new assessment instrument—the BICRO-39 scales. Arch Phys Med Rehabil. 1998;79(10):1213-1225. doi:10.1016/S0003-9993(98)90265-9. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0003-9993(98)90265-9
plain-language_description: The Brain Injury Community Rehabilitation Outcome-39 assesses a person’s community life after brain injury, including personal care, mobility, organization, work, social life, psychological functioning, and family relationships.

name: Functional Activities Questionnaire
description: "The Functional Activities Questionnaire (FAQ) is a collateral-report measure of difficulties in instrumental activities of daily living (IADLs)."
description_reference: González DA, Gonzales MM, Resch ZJ, et al. Comprehensive evaluation of the Functional Activities Questionnaire (FAQ) and its reliability and validity. Assessment. 2022;29(4):748-763. doi:10.1177/1073191121991215. PMCID: PMC8339133. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8339133/
plain-language_description: The Functional Activities Questionnaire asks a family member or other informant to rate how independently a person manages complex everyday tasks such as finances, shopping, meals, and appointments.

name: Functional Capacity Scale
description: The Functional Capacity Scale (FCS) assesses a patient's level of functioning and how much nursing support they need during hopsital care.  The scale has 12 markers: ambulation, alimentation, personal hygiene, physiological needs, life functions measurement (GCS), breathing, diagnosis, pre- and post-surgical treatment, dressing and drainage, acuteness of pain, pharmacotherapy, and neuropsychological outcome. For each marker, a patient may be classified into 1 of 4 groups: Group I (patient does not need assistance), group II (patient needs assistance), group III (patient needs significant help), and group IV (patient needs intensive care).
description_reference: Ślusarz R, Beuth W, Śniegocki M. Functional Capacity Scale as a new tool for early functional assessment in patients after surgical treatment of intracranial aneurysms. Med Sci Monit. 2012;18(11):CR680-CR686. doi:10.12659/MSM.883547. PMCID: PMC3560615. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3560615/
plain-language_description: The Functional Capacity Scale is a bedside scale that describes how much help a patient needs soon after aneurysm surgery, based on mobility, self-care, neurological status, breathing, and treatment needs.

name: Functional Independence Measure
description: "The Functional Independence Measure (FIM) is an 18-item, 7-level scale developed to uniformly assess severity of patient disability and medical rehabilitation functional outcome."
description_reference: Hamilton BB, Laughlin JA, Fiedler RC, Granger CV. Interrater reliability of the 7-level functional independence measure (FIM). Scand J Rehabil Med. 1994;26(3):115-119. PMID: 7801060. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7801060/
plain-language_description:
The Functional Independence Measure (FIM) is used to assess how much assistance a person needs to carry out activities of daily living.

It includes 18 activities covering both physical and cognitive tasks. These include:
1) Eating
2) Grooming
3) Bathing
4) Upper body dressing
5) Lower body dressing
6) Toileting
7) Bladder management
8) Bowel management
9) Bed to chair transfer
10) Toilet transfer
11) Shower transfer
12) Locomotion (ambulatory or wheelchair level)
13) Stairs
14) Cognitive comprehension
15) Expression
16) Social interaction
17) Problem solving
18) Memory

Each activity is rated on a 7-point scale, ranging from complete dependence to complete independence. The ratings are added together to give a total score from 18 to 126, with higher scores indicating greater independence and less need for assistance.

name: Functional Status Examination
description: "The Functional Status Examination (FSE) is a new measure designed to evaluate change in activities of everyday life as a function of an event or illness, including traumatic brain injury. The measure covers physical, social, and psychological domains. The FSE is based on a structured interview and includes levels of functioning that accommodate the full spectrum of possible outcomes, from death through recovery to preinjury functioning."
description_reference: Dikmen S, Machamer J, Miller B, Doctor J, Temkin N. Functional Status Examination: A New Instrument for Assessing Outcome in Traumatic Brain Injury. Journal of Neurotrauma. 2001;18(2):127-140. doi:10.1089/08977150150502578
plain-language_description:
The Functional Status Examination (FSE) is an interview-based assessment of how well a person is able to carry out everyday activities after a brain injury.

The FSE asks about 10 areas of everyday functioning, including: the physical domain - personal care, ambulation, and travel; the social domain - work or school, home management, leisure and recreation, social integration, and standard of living; the psychologic domain - cognitive and behavioural functioning, and financial independence. For each area, the person’s current abilities are compared with how they functioned before their brain injury.

Scores range from 0 (no change from previous functioning) to 3 (completely dependent or unable to perform the activity). The scores are added together to give a total score from 0 to 30, with higher scores reflecting poorer functioning. A score of 31 can be used for individuals who have died.

The interview also asks how bothersome the person finds their difficulties, and whether physical, cognitive, or emotional factors are contributing to them. If the person has returned to their previous level of functioning, they are asked about how long their recovery took.

name: Glasgow Outcome Scale extended
description: "To increase the sensitivity of the GOS, Jennett and colleagues later suggested that categories of outcome could be divided into upper and lower bands to create an expanded 8-point scale." The 8 categories are the following: dead, vegetative state, lower severe disability, upper severe disability, Lower moderate disability, upper moderate disability, lower good recovery, and upper good recovery"
description_reference: Wilson L, Boase K, Nelson LD, et al. A Manual for the Glasgow Outcome Scale-Extended Interview. Journal of Neurotrauma. 2021;38(17):2435-2446. doi:10.1089/neu.2020.7527
plain-language_description:
The Glasgow Outcome Scale–Extended (GOSe) is used to describe a person’s overall level of recovery and independence after a brain injury.

It is an expanded version of the Glasgow Outcome Scale and uses 8 levels of outcome, allowing for a more detailed assessment of recovery. These levels range from death and vegetative state, through severe and moderate disability, to good recovery. Higher GOSe categories indicate better recovery and greater independence in everyday life.

name: Karnofsky Performance Status Scale
description: "The Karnofsky Performance Status (KPS) is a widely used method to assess the functional status of a patient... The KPS describes a patient’s functional status as a comprehensive 11-point scale correlating to percentage values ranging from 100% (no evidence of disease, no symptoms) to 0% (death)."
description_reference: Péus, Dominik, et al. “Appraisal of the Karnofsky Performance Status and Proposal of a Simple Algorithmic System for Its Evaluation.” BMC Medical Informatics and Decision Making [London], vol. 13, no. 1, no. 72, July 2013, https://doi.org/10.1186/1472-6947-13-72.
plain-language_description: The Karnofsky Performance Status Scale (KPS) is used to describe a person's overall level of functioning. The scale considers whether the person can work or complete usual activities, care for themselves, and whether they need assistance or medical care. It uses scores from 0 to 100. A score of 100 represents normal functioning without symptoms or limitations, while lower scores reflect increasing difficulty with everyday activities and a greater need for assistance. A score of 0 represents death.

name: Modified Patient Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System Preference Scoring System
description: PROPr focuses on a subset of 7 PROMIS (Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System) domains to produce a scoring system for assgning values to health states. The 7 PROMIS domains included are: Cognitive Function – Abilities; Depression; Fatigue; Pain Interference; Physical Function; Sleep Disturbance; and Ability to Participate in Social Roles and Activities.
plain-language_description: The modified Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System Preference Scoring System (mPROPr) is used to summarize health outcomes based on responses to select PROMIS questionnaires. It combines information from seven areas of health: physical functioning, pain interference, fatigue, depression, sleep disturbance, cognitive functioning, and ability to participate in social roles and activities.
image: images/Modified Patient Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System Preference Scoring System.png

name: Modified Rankin Scale
description: "The modified Rankin Scale (mRS) is a single-item, global outcome rating scale that was developed to measure the degree of disability or dependence in the daily activities of people who have suffered from stroke or other neurological disorders...The mRS has a range between 0 and 6, where a score of 0 is ‘no symptoms at all’ and a score of 6 is ‘dead’; there are no subscales."
description_reference: Haggag, Hammazah, and Carol Hodgson. “Clinimetrics: Modified Rankin Scale (mRS).” Journal of Physiotherapy, vol. 68, no. 4, October 2022, pp. 281–281, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jphys.2022.05.017.
plain-language_description: A simple scale that measures how much a stroke or brain condition affects a person’s ability to handle daily activities and live independently. Scores range from 0 (no symptoms) to 6 (death).

name: Occupational Gaps Questionnaire
description: The Occupational Gaps Questionnaire measures a discrepancy between what they want to do and what they actually do.
description_reference:
Eriksson T, Jonsson H, Tham K, Eriksson G. A comparison of perceived occupational gaps between people with stress-related ill health or musculoskeletal pain and a reference group. Scand J Occup Ther. 2012;19(5):411-420. doi:10.3109/11038128.2011.620984. PMID: 22029609. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22029609/

Eriksson G, Tham K, Kottorp A. A cross-diagnostic validation of an instrument measuring participation in everyday occupations: the Occupational Gaps Questionnaire (OGQ). Scand J Occup Ther. 2013;20(2):152-160. doi:10.3109/11038128.2012.749944. PMID: 23216376. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23216376/
plain-language_description: It combines information from seven areas of health: physical functioning, pain interference, fatigue, depression, sleep disturbance, cognitive functioning, and ability to participate in social roles and activities.

name: Patient Competency Rating Scale
description: "The PCRS is a 30-item self-report questionnaire that asks patients and family members to make independent judgements about the perceived degree of competency the patient demonstrates on various behavioural, cognitive and emotional tasks. Comparison of patient ratings to family member ratings allows for insight into how realistic a patient is in evaluating his/her limitations."
description_reference: Borgaro, Susan R., and George P. Prigatano. “Modification of the Patient Competency Rating Scale for Use on an Acute Neurorehabilitation Unit: The PCRS-NR.” Brain Injury [London], vol. 17, no. 10, October 2003, pp. 847–53, https://doi.org/10.1080/0269905031000089350.
plain-language_description: The Patient Competency Rating Scale (PCRS) is a 30-item questionnaire used to assess how capable a person feels they are in carrying out everyday behavioural, cognitive, emotional, and functional tasks. The questionnaire can be completed separately by the patient and by a family member or other close person, which can help show whether the patient has an accurate awareness of their own strengths and difficulties.

name: Patient Reported Outcome Measures In Stroke - Subscles: Physical function, Satisfaction with social roles, Pain Interference, Fatigue, Anxiety, Depression, Sleep Disturbance
description_reference: Lens, Charlotte et al. “Patient Reported Outcomes Measurements Information System in Stroke Patients in Full and Shortened Format.” Frontiers in neurology vol. 11 630850. 22 Jan. 2021, doi:10.3389/fneur.2020.630850
plain-language_description: PROMIS® (Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System®) is a set of person-centered measures that evaluates and monitors physical, mental, and social health in adults and children. PROMIS measures are generic, rather than disease-specific, and can be used with the general population and with individuals living with chronic conditions.

name: Physical Performance Test
description: "The Physical Performance Test (PPT) assesses multiple domains of physical function using observed performance of tasks that simulate activities of daily living."
description_reference: Reuben DB, Siu AL. An objective measure of physical function of elderly outpatients: The Physical Performance Test. J Am Geriatr Soc. 1990;38(10):1105-1112. doi:10.1111/j.1532-5415.1990.tb01373.x. PMID: 2229864. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2229864/
plain-language_description: The Physical Performance Test (PPT) is a performance-based assessment of how well a person can carry out everyday physical activities. During the test, the person is asked to complete a series of practical tasks, such as walking, dressing, picking up an object, and other mobility or self-care activities. An assessor observes how the tasks are performed and assigns a score based on the person’s performance.

name: Role Resumption List
description: The Role Resumption List "assesses changes in amount and quality of activities compared with premorbid levels" in work, social relations, leisure activities, and mobility.
description_reference: Spikman JM, Boelen DHE, Lamberts KF, Brouwer WH, Fasotti L. Effects of a multifaceted treatment program for executive dysfunction after acquired brain injury on indications of executive functioning in daily life. J Int Neuropsychol Soc. 2010;16(1):118-129. doi:10.1017/S1355617709991020. PMID: 19900348. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19900348/ Buunk AM, Groen RJM, Veenstra WS, Spikman JM. Leisure and social participation in patients 4-10 years after aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage. Brain Inj. 2015;29(13-14):1589-1596. doi:10.3109/02699052.2015.1073789. PMID: 26362688. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26362688/
plain-language_description: The Role Resumption List uses a structured interview to compare a person’s current work, social relationships, leisure activities, and mobility with their participation before the brain injury.

name: Screening of symptoms in subarachnoid hemorrhage
description: " The SOS-SAH was developed to cover relevant PROs for patients successfully treated after an aSAH. The SOS-SAH consists of 40 items covering 14 domains, and an additional section for a proxy measurement."
description_reference: Nobels-Janssen E, Abma IL, Verhagen WIM, Bartels RHMA, van der Wees PJ, Boogaarts JD. Development of a patient-reported outcome measure for patients who have recovered from a subarachnoid hemorrhage: the "questionnaire for the screening of symptoms in aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage" (SOS-SAH). BMC Neurol. 2021 Apr 16;21(1):162.https://doi.org/10.1186/s12883-021-02184-x
plain-language_description:
The Screening of Symptoms in Subarachnoid Hemorrhage (SOS-SAH) is a patient-reported questionnaire developed specifically for people who have experienced an aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (aSAH). It is designed to identify ongoing symptoms and difficulties that may not be obvious during routine follow-up visits.

The questionnaire contains 40 questions covering 14 areas, including cognitive difficulties, sensitivity to stimuli, anxiety, depression, fatigue, social participation, personality changes, language, vision, taste, smell, hearing, headache, and sexual functioning.

The person reports their own symptoms and experiences, helping patients and healthcare professionals identify concerns that may need further discussion, treatment, or support. The SOS-SAH also includes a short section that can be completed by a family member or other close person to provide additional information about cognitive functioning and personality changes.
image: images/Screening of symptoms in aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage.png

name: Short Form Health Survey
description:
"The SF-36 includes one multi-item scale that assesses eight health concepts."
"Regression methods were used to select and score 12 items from the Medical Outcomes Study 36-Item Short-Form Health Survey (SF-36)."
description_reference:
Ware JE Jr, Sherbourne CD. The MOS 36-item short-form health survey (SF-36). I. Conceptual framework and item selection. Med Care. 1992;30(6):473-483. PMID: 1593914. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1593914/

Ware J Jr, Kosinski M, Keller SD. A 12-Item Short-Form Health Survey: construction of scales and preliminary tests of reliability and validity. Med Care. 1996;34(3):220-233. doi:10.1097/00005650-199603000-00003. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8628042/
plain-language_description: The SF-12 and SF-36 questionnaires ask how a person’s health affects physical activity, everyday roles, pain, energy, social life, and emotional well-being. The SF-12 is the shorter version.

name: Subarachnoid Haemorrhage Outcome Tool
description: "The final SAHOT included 56 items dealing with cognitive, physical, and behavioural/psychological consequences of subarachnoid haemorrhage... The SAHOT offers the first subarachnoid haemorrhage-specific scientifically robust outcome measure with potential utility in neurovascular clinical services and research studies."
description_reference: Pace, Adrian, et al. “A Subarachnoid Haemorrhage-Specific Outcome Tool.” Brain (London, England : 1878) [England], vol. 141, no. 4, April 2018, pp. 1111–21, https://doi.org/10.1093/brain/awy003.
plain-language_description: A 56-question checklist designed specifically for people who have had a subarachnoid haemorrhage. The tool looks at the impact of the condition on general aspects of daily life, behavioral aspects, mental aspects, and physical aspects.

name: Unnamed 'rating scale' - Self + Proxy versions
description: "In order to assess functional impairments in daily life, an ad hoc scale for patients' self-rating and a parallel version for rating the complaints of the patients by their life-companions were developed. The first two items cover: the activities of daily living of the patients and are related to a feeling of insecurity in social relations and a reduction in free-time activities. The next two items are related to a possible reduction in mental capacity and concentration. A further two items refer to problems with activation, the first of which related to a reduction of interest for daily problems (indifference) and the second item is related to a loss of motivation. The next items cover problems in sensorimotor fine coordination and sleeping problems. The items were rated by the patient on a 5-point scale. Therefore, a patient could reach a maximum impairment score of 40...We additionally employed a parallel questionnaire for the partners of the patients. The items covered areas identical to those in the patient self-rating questionnaire."
description_reference: Hutter, BO and Gilsbach, JM. Introspective Capacities in Patients with Cognitive Deficits after Subarachnoid Hemorrhage. Journal of Clinical and Experimental Neuropsychology, 1995; 17(4): 499-517.
plain-language_description:
This unnamed rating scale was developed to assess difficulties with everyday functioning after illness or injury. It includes a patient self-report version and a matching proxy version completed by a family member.

The scale asks about several areas of daily life, including activities of daily living, social confidence, leisure activities, mental ability and concentration, interest and motivation, fine motor coordination, and sleep.

Each item is rated on a 5-point scale, with higher scores indicating greater impairment. Scores can be added together to give an overall impairment score, with a maximum score of 40.

Because the patient and proxy versions cover the same areas, their responses can also be compared to provide different perspectives on the patient’s day-to-day difficulties.

name: Work Limitations Questionnaire
description: The Work Limitations Questionnaire was developed "for measuring the on-the-job impact of chronic health problems and/or treatment (work limitations)."
description_reference: Lerner D, Amick BC 3rd, Rogers WH, Malspeis S, Bungay K, Cynn D. The Work Limitations Questionnaire. Med Care. 2001;39(1):72-85. doi:10.1097/00005650-200101000-00009. PMID: 11176545. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11176545/
plain-language_description: The Work Limitations Questionnaire is a self-report questionnaire used to understand how a person's health affects their ability to perform their job. The original version includes 25 questions covering four areas: time management, physical demands, mental and interpersonal demands, and meeting work output demands. Scale score range from 0 % (limited none of the time) to 100 % (limited all of the time).

name: Glasgow Outcome Scale
description: "A five-point scale is described—death, persistent vegetative state, severe disability, moderate disability, and good recovery. Duration as well as intensity of disability should be included in an index of ill-health; this applies particularly after head injury, because many disabled survivors are young."
description_reference: Jennett, Bryan, and Michael Bond. “ASSESSMENT OF OUTCOME AFTER SEVERE BRAIN DAMAGE: A Practical Scale.” The Lancet (British Edition), vol. 305, no. 7905, March 1975, pp. 480–84, https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(75)92830-5.
plain-language_description: The Glasgow Outcome Scale (GOS) is a five-level scale used to describe a person’s overall recovery after a brain injury. It classifies outcomes from death through to good recovery. It includes five categories: death, persistent vegetative state, severe disability, moderate disability, and good recovery.

name: Health Utilities Index Mark 3
description: There are 2 versions of the HUI. The HUI Mark II (HUI-2) measures sensation, mobility, emotion, cognition, self-care, and pain. The HUI Mark III (HUI-3) measures vision, hearing, speech, ambulation, dexterity, emotion, cognition, and pain.
description_reference: Thompson, Nicolas R., Brittany R. Lapin, and Irene L. Katzan. "Utilities estimated from PROMIS scales for cost-effectiveness analyses in stroke." Medical Decision Making 43.6 (2023): 704-718.
plain-language_description: The Health Utilities Index (HUI) is a questionnaire used to measure a person's overall physical, mental, and emotional quality of life. It comes in two main versions: HUI-2 and HUI-3.

name: Home-time
description: Home-time measures the number of days a patient is alive and at their private residence after stroke, typically within 90 days of admission. Derived objectively from routinely collected linked health records, it is proposed as a patient-centred surrogate for functional status. It enables large-scale assessment without requiring patient or proxy responses, reducing follow-up burden and supporting inclusion of patients who may face barriers to research participation.
description_reference: Gattellari, Melina, et al. "Measuring stroke outcomes for 74 501 patients using linked administrative data: System‐wide estimates and validation of ‘home‐time’as a surrogate measure of functional status." International Journal of Clinical Practice 74.6 (2020): e13484.
plain-language_description: Home-time counts how many days a person lives at home in the 90 days after being admitted to the hospital for a stroke.

name: Lawton Instrumental Activities of Daily Living  Scale
description: "The Lawton Instrumental Activities of Daily Living (IADL) Scale assesses a person’s ability to perform tasks such as using a telephone."
description_reference: Graf C. The Lawton instrumental activities of daily living scale. Am J Nurs. 2008;108(4):52-62. doi:10.1097/01.NAJ.0000314810.46029.74. PMID: 18367931. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18367931/ Original instrument: Lawton MP, Brody EM. Assessment of older people: self-maintaining and instrumental activities of daily living. Gerontologist. 1969;9(3):179-186. PMID: 5349366. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/5349366/
plain-language_description: The Lawton Instrumental Activities of Daily Living Scale checks whether a person can independently manage complex everyday tasks such as shopping, cooking, transportation, medicines, and money.

name: Middle Cerebral Artery Neurol Scale
description: The 10 MCANS items reflect 21 ordinal degrees of severity. The items include consciousness, speech/verbal communication, eye movements/eyes and head shift, facial palsy, arm: motor power/raising, hand: motor power/raising, leg: motor power/raising, foot dorsiflexion, upper limb tone, lower limb tone. "The MCANS items are summed to create a total score ranging form 0 to 100."
description_reference: Edwards, Dorothy F., Yu-Wen Chen MSW, and Michael N. Diringer. "Unified Neurological Stroke Scale is valid in ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke." Stroke 26.10 (1995): 1852-1858.
plain-language_description: The MCANS (Middle Cerebral Artery Neurological Scale) is a 10-item checklist doctors use to measure how severely a stroke has affected a patient's body and brain function.

name: National Institute of Health Stroke Scale
description: "The National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) is a 15-item impairment scale used to measure stroke severity...The NIHSS includes the following domains: level of consciousness, eye movements, integrity of visual fields, facial movements, arm and leg muscle strength, sensation, coordination, language, speech and neglect. Each impairment is scored on an ordinal scale ranging from 0 to 2, 0 to 3, or 0 to 4. Item scores are summed to a total score ranging from 0 to 42 (the higher the score, the more severe the stroke)."
description_reference: Kwah, Li Khim, and Joanna Diong. “National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS).” Journal of Physiotherapy [Netherlands], vol. 60, no. 1, March 2014, pp. 61–61, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jphys.2013.12.012.

name: Scandinavian Neurological Stroke Scale
description: The SNSS yields three separate scores: prognostic (SNSS-PRG), long-term (SNSS-LT), and a total score. The prognostic score includes consciousness, gaze palsy, and limb strength. The long-term score items evaluate limb strength, dysphasia, facial palsy, orientation, and gait.
description_reference: Edwards, Dorothy F., Yu-Wen Chen MSW, and Michael N. Diringer. "Unified Neurological Stroke Scale is valid in ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke." Stroke 26.10 (1995): 1852-1858.
plain-language_description: The Scandinavian Neurological Stroke Scale (SNSS) is a tool doctors use to check a patient's physical and mental recovery after a stroke. It provides three main scores: a prognostic score (to estimate short-term outlook), a long-term score (to evaluate ongoing recovery), and a total score.

name: Short-Physical Performance Battery Score
description: "[T]he domains of balance and gait are explored also by the Short-Physical Performance Battery (SPPB). This is a widely used scale exploring the reduction of physical performance in older persons, particularly muscle strength of lower extremities, 4-m walking speed at usual pace, and balance. It has the ability of predicting mobility-disability, nursing home and hospital admission. Poor physical performance and balance alterations are among the main causes of falls in older individuals."
description_reference: Lauretani, F., Ticinesi, A., Gionti, L. et al. Short-Physical Performance Battery (SPPB) score is associated with falls in older outpatients. Aging Clin Exp Res 31, 1435–1442 (2019). https://doi.org/10.1007/s40520-018-1082-y

name: Stroke symptom checklist
description: An informal checklist of 12 common symptoms (including effects of mood, cognition and physical problems) associated with brain injury. These were identified at the time by local clinicians. Patients score a point if symptoms are worse now than prior to their illness. Scores range from 0 to 12.
description_reference: Quinn, Audrey C., et al. "Self-perceived health status following aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage: a cohort study." BMJ open 4.4 (2014): e003932.
plain-language_description: The Stroke Symptom Checklist (SSC) is an informal 12-question tool used to track changes in a person's physical and mental health after a stroke or brain injury.
